record.title: Short token cues elicit reasoning behavior associated with training data in tested base models
record.summary: An arXiv preprint reports that prefilling selected response-opening tokens can raise tested base models’ math accuracy toward that of direct-RL counterparts, and controlled data edits can make arbitrary openings act as reasoning cues. The results support a training-association mechanism in the tested models, while leaving the contribution of RL, generalization and cue-conditioned safety unresolved.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In the authors’ tested settings, prefilling selected two-token openings raised base-model MATH-500 pass@1 from 42% to 78% for Olmo-3-7B (the compared RL-Zero model scored 75%) and from 72% to 87% for Qwen3-14B (matching its compared RL variant). The authors report gains across several math benchmarks; the Qwen coding result stayed near its base-model level.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report controlled mid-training data edits that made previously ineffective tokens such as “chicken” elicit reasoning behavior in Olmo-3-7B; a similar instruction/data edit made “Think duck duck goose” perform comparably to “Think step by step” in their tested setting.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: These experiments do not establish that reinforcement learning adds no reasoning capability, that the reported effects generalize to deployed instruction models, or that any cue is broadly safe; the authors report cue-dependent refusal and harmful-compliance behavior.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent reproduction of the main cue and data-intervention results has been inspected.

Paper §2.1 describes beam proposal over 30 MATH training problems, while the pinned initial public code defaults to 100 beam proposals and 30 screening problems; the configuration that produced published figures is unresolved.
Safety behavior is a cue-specific author-run case study; broader prompt/model coverage and independent adjudication are unavailable.

brief.importance_rationale: If sustained, the result would change how researchers interpret reasoning gains from direct RL and could make training-data associations a practical control surface. Evidence is limited to selected base models and author-run settings, so it is meaningful rather than field-settling.
limitations: All performance and data-intervention measurements are reported by the preprint authors; the research desk has not independently reproduced them.
Main cue comparisons use selected openings on Olmo-3-7B and Qwen3-14B with specified prompts and up to 32 sampled responses per problem; cue effectiveness varies by model and prompt.
The paper/code mismatch on beam-search problem count leaves the figure-producing configuration unresolved.
The RL comparison is direct base-to-R1-Zero-style training and does not establish what multi-stage post-training adds.
The safety evidence is a cue-specific case study, not a general safety rate; cues can change refusal and harmful compliance.
brief.summary: An arXiv preprint reports that prefilling selected response-opening tokens can raise tested base models’ math accuracy toward that of direct-RL counterparts, and controlled data edits can make arbitrary openings act as reasoning cues. The results support a training-association mechanism in the tested models, while leaving the contribution of RL, generalization and cue-conditioned safety unresolved.

technical.claimed_result: For Olmo-3-7B, the selected cue raises MATH-500 pass@1 from 42% to 78% versus 75% for the compared RL-Zero model; for Qwen3-14B it rises from 72% to 87%, matching the compared RL variant. Controlled mid-training edits make selected arbitrary cues elicit reasoning in the authors’ tested models. These are preprint-reported results, not independently reproduced.
technical.demonstrated_result: The inspected primary preprint reports cue-conditioned performance and controlled data-edit experiments. the research desk has not run the models or reproduced the experiments; the reported outcomes remain CLAIMED.
technical.mechanism: A short fixed opening changes which continuation distribution the base model samples. The authors report that direct RL increases probability of selected openings, and counterfactual data edits can change which tokens cue reasoning. This is evidence for learned token-to-behavior associations in the studied regimes, not proof that RL only changes opening tokens.
technical.regime: Authors’ experiments on Olmo-3-7B and Qwen3-14B with selected two-token openings, math/coding benchmarks and 32 responses per problem; data-edit retraining on Olmo-3-7B and SmolLM3-3B. The paper’s direct comparisons are base models versus direct RL-style counterparts.
technical.strongest_baseline: The paper compares each base model without a cue and its selected-cue version with its RL-trained counterpart. On MATH-500 the reported rates are 42% / 78% / 75% for Olmo-3-7B and 72% / 87% / 87% for Qwen3-14B.

brief.title: Short token cues elicit reasoning behavior associated with training data in tested base models
brief.why_it_matters: The results make a concrete case that some reasoning behavior in these tested models can be elicited through short output openings associated with training data, complicating simple claims about what direct RL newly teaches. If replicated, this would affect post-training interpretation and evaluation design. The experiments do not establish broad deployment transfer or that RL adds no capability.
